extracted.intended_audience: IP office staff, policymakers, researchers and statisticians working on industrial design and trademark statistics and policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for (a) what makes an industrial design eligible for protection and how offices examine applications, and (b) the statistical/measurement conventions used to report industrial design filing, registration and procedural data across IP offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial design eligibility criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: For an industrial design to be eligible for protection, it typically needs to meet criteria such as being new, original and of an individual character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination procedures vary widely between offices: some offices carry out no search and no substantive examination prior to registration, while others conduct a substantive examination checking the design against designs on the register for novelty and/or originality. This affects whether and how the 'new, original and individual character' criteria are applied in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in substantive examination practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Offices differ in whether they perform substantive examination (novelty/originality checks) or only perform formalities/no search prior to registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because examination approaches differ, examination outcome distributions (registered, rejected, withdrawn/abandoned) and pendency measures are not directly comparable across offices without caution. The report explicitly warns that examination procedures vary and advises care when comparing offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term/duration of industrial design rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial design rights generally last for up to 15 years from the date an application is filed, although they last up to 25 years in most European countries and up to 10 years in China.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a substantive legal/regulatory variation that affects active registrations and renewal/maintenance analyses; users should account for jurisdictional differences when comparing 'registrations in force' across offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of 'application design counts' for comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics based on the number of designs contained in industrial design applications—known as application design counts—improve worldwide comparability by harmonizing data between offices that allow several designs in a single application and those that allow only one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use application design counts (rather than raw application counts) to harmonize filing statistics across offices with different rules on multiple-design applications; the report recommends this as the preferred basis for international comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office data versus origin data (resident vs abroad distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications received by offices (office data) provide information on the destination of industrial design activity, whereas applications filed by applicants at their home office(s) (origin data) provide information on the source of industrial design activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both views complement each other: office data show where filings occur, origin data show where applicants reside. Analyses of filing flows, activity abroad and domestic intensity should specify which data type is used and be mindful of differences (e.g., Hague vs direct filings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hague System and filing-route attribution for non-resident activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague System filing route accounted for approximately one-third (33.6%) of global non-resident filing activity in 2023; the remaining two-thirds were filed directly at offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing non-resident filing patterns, distinguish Hague-designated filings from direct filings because route influences coverage, comparability and interpretation of cross-border filing activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of per-GDP and per-capita normalization for intensity comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjusting resident filing activity according to GDP and population helps when comparing the intensity of resident industrial design filing across origins (e.g., resident design counts per USD 100 billion of GDP, per million population).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normalized metrics reveal activity relative to development level and facilitate fairer cross-country comparisons; the report highlights examples (e.g., China highest per USD 100 billion GDP, Republic of Korea highest per million population) and notes changes over time should be interpreted relative to such normalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification/grouping of designs by Locarno classes into industry sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Grouping the 32 Locarno classes into 12 industry sectors serves to highlight the most important industry sectors for designs contained within industrial design applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the sector grouping (textiles & accessories; furniture & household goods; tools & machines; electricity & lighting; ICT & audiovisual; etc.) to analyse sectoral concentration and the top sectors for offices or origins; the report gives breakdowns and cautions that sectoral top-three shares vary by office/origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key procedural and performance metrics for offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural metrics collected and reported include: total applications processed, registered, total rejections, withdrawn/abandoned, applications pending, number of examiners (FTE), first office action days, and final office decision days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics are used to compare office performance and outcomes, but the report warns that procedural differences and reporting incompleteness make full harmonization difficult; exercise caution when making cross-office comparisons and note that some totals may be incomplete due to omitted elements by offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of potentially pending applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Potentially pending applications are taken to be all industrial design applications, at any stage in the process, awaiting a final decision by an office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting backlog or workload, include all applications awaiting final decision. The report provides examples (US had the largest number in 2023) and links pending counts to procedural differences (e.g., offices with substantive examination may exhibit different pending profiles).
